context: macOS is a stated target but there is no Mac to test on and notarisation costs $99/yr
alternatives: (a) buy Apple Developer account (b) CI-only unsigned (c) defer macOS to Phase 2
evidence: Gatekeeper blocks unsigned apps; GitHub macos-14 runners can build but not interactively verify
selected: (b) CI-only, ad-hoc signed
consequences: Users see a Gatekeeper warning and need the right-click-open workaround; interactive macOS behaviour is unverified

context: Project licence determines which OSINT tools can legally be bundled
alternatives: (a) proprietary/source-available (b) GPL-3.0 (c) MIT/Apache-2.0
evidence: Neo4j is AGPL; holehe is GPL-3.0; theHarvester has no licence at all; ExifTool is GPL/Artistic
selected: (a) proprietary/source-available
consequences: Rules out Neo4j, holehe, and bundling ExifTool. Forces pure-Rust extraction and an external-handoff tier. Keeps future options open.

context: Whether Phase 1 must support distribution to third parties
alternatives: (a) personal use first (b) distribute from day one
evidence: Connector signing, permission diffs, revocation and quarantine are substantial work
selected: (a) personal use first
consequences: Connector signing and revocation move to Phase 2/3; Phase 1 ships built-in and declarative connectors only. Architecture still designed for distribution so this is not a rewrite later.

context: Model and dataset downloads need explicit approval under the implementation discipline
alternatives: (a) pre-approve a named list (b) approve case by case
evidence: Blocking every AI increment on a separate approval would stall the media and AI work entirely
selected: (a) pre-approved: bge-small int8, CLIP ViT-B/32, Tesseract eng, z0-z6 world PMTiles, free Steam Web API key
consequences: AI, OCR, media and map increments are unblocked. Models are downloaded at runtime and never committed. ODbL attribution is mandatory for the map tiles.

context: Building vendored OpenSSL on Windows requires a native Windows perl; cygwin perls are rejected
alternatives: (a) install Strawberry Perl (b) CI-only verification of the storage layer (c) re-open ADR-0004 and drop SQLCipher
evidence: msys64 perl fails with 'doesn't produce Windows like paths'; Git perl lacks Locale::Maketext::Simple; no mature OpenSSL-free SQLCipher binding exists in Rust
selected: (a) install Strawberry Perl
consequences: Documented README prerequisite; CI verifies perl before building so the failure is legible. Local builds work normally.

context: Minimum supported end-user hardware, which decides whether embeddings are on by default
alternatives: (a) 8GB RAM no discrete GPU (b) 16GB with GPU
evidence: Not yet measured; depends on PoC P2 and P7 results
selected: undecided
consequences: Determines whether local embeddings and image similarity are default-on or opt-in, and the CPU-only AI fallback profile

context: Install-size ceiling
alternatives: (a) ~15MB Tauri only (b) ~150MB with ONNX and embedding models (c) ~250MB adding Tesseract and a world basemap
evidence: Owner has previously been burned by a 1.45GB bundle; models are downloaded at runtime rather than bundled, which softens this
selected: undecided
consequences: Constrains whether models ship in the installer or download on first use

context: Strength of the adversary model
alternatives: (a) hobbyist keeping tidy notes (b) journalist protecting sources from a state actor
evidence: Not derivable from the spec
selected: undecided
consequences: Decides memory zeroization scope, whether swap hygiene and locked pages are required, whether an OS keychain option may exist at all, and whether shipping without an external security audit is defensible

context: Hardware token or OS biometric unlock in scope, or passphrase only
alternatives: (a) passphrase only (b) add OS biometric (c) add hardware token
evidence: Passphrase-only is assumed for increment 2
selected: assumed (a) passphrase only
consequences: If biometric or token unlock is wanted later, the key hierarchy in kokin-keys already supports additional key-wrapping paths, so this is additive

context: Whether outputs may ever be used in a legal proceeding
alternatives: (a) no (b) yes
evidence: The audit chain is tamper-evident, not tamper-proof, and must not be called chain of custody
selected: assumed (a) no
consequences: If yes, the 'not chain of custody' language needs review by a lawyer rather than an architect, and RFC-3161 timestamping moves forward from Phase 3

context: Development hours available per week
alternatives: (a) evenings/weekends (b) full time
evidence: Determines whether the 12-increment plan to the vertical slice is roughly three months or twelve
selected: undecided
consequences: Only affects scheduling, not scope or sequence

context: The WhatsMyName dataset is licensed CC BY-SA 4.0, not MIT. PoC P8 planned to port wmn-data.json into Kokin's declarative connector format, which is an adaptation of a ShareAlike work inside a source-available product.
alternatives: (a) ship wmn-data.json verbatim as a separate file with attribution and licence notice, keeping our code proprietary (b) transform it into our format and release only that derived file under CC BY-SA (c) fetch it at runtime and never redistribute it (d) build our own site list from scratch (e) drop username enumeration
evidence: GitHub reports NOASSERTION; the LICENSE.md text retrieved via the API reads verbatim Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International. ShareAlike attaches to Adapted Material, not to separately distributed works, so this is narrower than GPL linking but is not nothing.
selected: undecided - P8 is blocked on this
consequences: Option (a) is lowest risk and needs no legal opinion. Option (b) is workable but means publishing a derived data file under BY-SA, which the owner may not want. Whether a curated list of sites and detection rules attracts copyright or EU database right at all is a genuine legal question this project should not answer for itself.

context: Five rust-unic crates are unmaintained with no upgrade path, reaching us only through Tauri. cargo-deny 0.20 cannot express an expiry on an ignore entry.
alternatives: (a) ignore by advisory ID and track expiry in the risk register (b) set the unmaintained policy to workspace-only (c) fail the build until Tauri drops urlpattern
evidence: RustSec states no safe upgrade is available. The crates are static Unicode property tables performing no I/O.
selected: (a) ignore by ID
consequences: Any other unmaintained crate still fails the build, which (b) would not achieve. The cost is that the suppression never lapses on its own; R-013 carries the review date and this is stated in deny.toml.

context: ADR-0007 mandates YAML for the confidence scales, but serde_yaml is deprecated and its successors are an ambiguous field of forks
alternatives: (a) yaml_serde by The YAML Organization (b) serde_norway (c) serde-saphyr (d) generate Rust from the YAML in a Python lint and take no Rust YAML dependency (e) hand-roll a parser for the subset we author
evidence: Measured, not assumed: yaml_serde pulls libyaml-rs with ~240 unsafe blocks; serde_norway pulls unsafe-libyaml-norway with ~248; serde-saphyr is pure Rust (granit-parser has 1) but adds 9 transitive crates concentrated in one maintainer and reached 1.0 only recently. All four are MIT OR Apache-2.0. The existing lint scripts are Python-stdlib-only, so (d) would mean adding PyYAML to CI or hand-rolling a parser anyway.
selected: (a) yaml_serde
consequences: The unsafe count does not decide this, because the parser only ever sees bytes embedded at compile time from our own repo — no user, case, or network input reaches it. What decides it is which fork survives, so institutional provenance wins. If scales ever become user-supplied, this must be revisited and (c) becomes the right answer. Swap cost is one module: crates/kokin-graph/src/scales.rs.

context: ADR-0003 calls for FTS5 over observations, entities, notes and claims, but those are four differently-shaped tables and FTS5 external content addresses exactly one
alternatives: (a) one search_document projection table with FTS5 external content over it (b) a contentless index (content='') storing terms only (c) one FTS5 table per source table (d) a plain (non-external) FTS5 table holding its own copy of the text
evidence: Measured on the bundled SQLite 3.51.3: external content creates no search_index_content shadow table, confirming it keeps no second copy of the text, whereas (d) would. (b) is smaller still but cannot produce snippet() at all, because a contentless index has no text to excerpt. (c) multiplies the trigger surface by four and makes a ranked result list across kinds a UNION that cannot be ranked coherently.
selected: (a) projection plus external content
consequences: One copy of the text exists beyond the origin row, which is the price of snippets; the index remains a pure projection and rebuild() reproduces it from the case. subject_kind is deliberately left unconstrained so indexing a new kind of thing is one more trigger rather than a table rebuild, since SQLite cannot ALTER a CHECK.

context: A search document could carry text belonging to rows it does not own - most temptingly, indexing a relationship by the display names of the entities it joins, since 'Acme director' is what an analyst would actually type
alternatives: (a) index only the text a row owns (b) denormalise endpoint names into the relationship document (c) denormalise, plus triggers that refresh every dependent document when an entity is renamed
evidence: (b) is measurably wrong: the test a_relationship_carries_only_the_text_it_owns renames an endpoint and asserts no relationship document retains the old name. (c) is correct but the refresh trigger must recompute a join for every edge touching the renamed entity, and any table later added to the borrow graph silently needs its own refresh path.
selected: (a) a document carries only the text its own row owns
consequences: Searching an entity name does not surface its relationships directly; reaching an edge means finding an endpoint and following it, which is stated as a known limitation. In exchange no document can be stale with respect to a row it does not control, so a rename can never leave a name searchable that the case no longer holds.

context: Indexing page prose makes text volume unbounded by document structure: half a gigabyte of paragraphs holds no more links or titles than a small page, but chunking it produces hundreds of thousands of observations and trips max_observations, so a document that used to be read starts being refused
alternatives: (a) truncate prose at a byte budget and report the truncation (b) refuse the document, consistent with the existing observation cap (c) raise max_observations to accommodate prose (d) one observation per document holding all its text
evidence: Measured: the existing hostile-corpus test a_500_mb_document_is_read_in_bounded_memory began failing with TooManyObservations the moment prose was indexed at 1 KiB chunks. (c) does not fix it - no fixed cap survives an arbitrarily long document. (d) breaks max_value_bytes on anything substantial and gives a locator spanning the whole file, which routes a hit to nowhere useful.
selected: (a) truncate and report, at 4 MiB of prose in 4 KiB chunks
consequences: Splits from the observation cap deliberately: too many discrete facts means a truncated fact list that reads as complete, so refusal is right; prose is a search aid, and refusing a document over its wordiness would also discard every link, title and address in it. The residual risk is A-022 - text_truncated_bytes reaches the caller and the audit log but not yet the analyst at search time.

context: Reporting which documents a case has not read needs to know which artifacts a run was about. derivation records what a run produced, and a run that produced nothing - a refused PDF, a blown limit, an empty document - writes no edge at all, so it is indistinguishable from an artifact nobody has opened
alternatives: (a) a run_subject table recording what each run took as input (b) infer attempts from derivation edges alone (c) infer them from the audit chain, which already logs evidence.extracted per artifact (d) add a subject column to transform_run
evidence: a_document_read_and_found_empty_is_not_a_document_nobody_read fails under (b): a real extraction of <html></html> produces zero observations and zero derivations. (c) makes the audit log a queryable data store, and the audit payload carries no run_id so a gap could not name the run accountable for it. (d) is impossible without editing a shipped migration, which this project does not do.
selected: (a) run_subject, written before anything can fail, so it survives every path out of extraction
consequences: One more row per run, and a second place lineage must be kept honest. In exchange 'attempted and found nothing' is distinguishable from 'never attempted' - finished work from a job still to do. Upgraded cases can only recover attempts that left a derivation edge, so they under-report attempts until re-extraction; the error direction is deliberate and pinned by a test, reporting work as still to do and never as already done.

context: A re-extraction produces a second reading of the same document, and its account of what it failed to cover replaces the earlier one. A gap the latest run fixed must stop being reported, or the case keeps apologising for a shortfall that no longer exists and the report becomes noise
alternatives: (a) report only gaps belonging to the latest run over each subject (b) a coverage_gap_supersession table mirroring observation_supersession (c) mark earlier gaps resolved on rerun
evidence: (b) and (c) both fail the case that matters most - a rerun that covers everything writes no gap row, so there is nothing to point a supersession at and nothing to mark resolved. a_rerun_that_reads_the_whole_document_clears_the_gap covers exactly that. (c) additionally requires mutating an append-only lineage table.
selected: (a) gaps are scoped to the latest run, so supersession needs no rows of its own
consequences: Every coverage query carries a window function over run_subject joined to transform_run, which is small next to the documents it describes. Correctness now depends on ordering runs correctly, which is not free: started_utc is second-resolution, run ids are random, and the tie must be broken on rowid - see A-023 for what breaks when it is not. Earlier gaps stay on record, so a case can still be asked what it used to be unable to answer.

context: ADR-0008 requires reads to resolve identity through er_merge_map. Whether that map may be more than one level deep decides whether resolution is an indexed lookup or a recursive walk, and whether a cycle is representable at all
alternatives: (a) enforce depth 1 with triggers, so a canonical is always a root and an absorbed entity always a leaf (b) allow chains and resolve with a recursive CTE (c) allow chains and rewrite ancestors when a canonical is itself merged
evidence: (b) makes A -> B plus B -> A two ordinary-looking merges and an infinite loop in every query that reads identity, over rows an analyst can toggle at will; preventing that needs a recursive check inside a trigger. (c) rewrites merge-map rows, which breaks split - deactivating a rewritten row no longer restores the state it was written from. the_merge_map_cannot_be_made_to_chain_or_to_cycle covers all four ways in, including the reactivation path.
selected: (a) depth 1, enforced from both ends and on reactivation
consequences: canonical_id is one indexed lookup and a cycle is unrepresentable rather than merely unlikely. The cost moves to the API: joining two clusters is deactivate-then-insert across every member, inside one decision and one transaction. Merging two entities that each already have clusters therefore writes as many rows as the losing cluster has members.

context: Merging two entities has to pick which one survives as the canonical, and the choice is visible to the analyst as the name that remains
alternatives: (a) the older entity, by created_utc then rowid (b) the entity named first in the call (c) the lexicographically smaller id (d) ask the analyst every time
evidence: created_utc alone cannot decide it - it is second-resolution and one extraction creates many entities inside one second - and entity ids are random hex, so (c) and the obvious tie-break for (a) both make the survivor a coin flip. Two tests failed intermittently before this was found, the same root cause as A-023. (b) makes the result depend on which of two identical-looking rows an analyst clicked first.
selected: (a) older first, tie-broken on rowid, which is insertion order
consequences: The same case rebuilt from the same sequence of merges displays the same name, which (b) and (c) do not give. Either choice produces a correct cluster, so this is reproducibility rather than correctness - but an analyst should not have to look to find out which name won. (d) remains available later as an override and is not foreclosed.

context: The same ordering defect - a second-resolution timestamp broken on a random id - has now been written three times in three crates, each time found by a test failing intermittently rather than by review. evidence_for was the third, and its doc comment promised insertion order while delivering a coin flip
alternatives: (a) fix the occurrence and add a lint that fails the build on the pattern (b) fix the occurrence and rely on review (c) give every table a monotonic id column so the reflex becomes correct (d) make *_utc columns sub-second so ties stop being the normal case
evidence: Three occurrences is a pattern. (b) is what was in place for the first two and did not catch either; both were found by a flaky test, which is the expensive way. (c) is a schema change across every shipped migration, which this project does not do, and would still leave the existing columns wrong. (d) narrows the window without closing it and does nothing for rows written inside one transaction. The lint was A/B tested by reintroducing both real historical bugs and catches both, including the multi-line window-function form.
selected: (a) scripts/lint_sql_ordering.py, run in CI, rejecting ORDER BY <col>_utc followed by an id tie-break
consequences: The wrong version stops being writable rather than merely being wrong, which matters because it reads as obviously correct - that is why it kept being written. The lint is textual and knows nothing about SQL, so a genuinely monotonic id column would be a false positive; audit_event.id is the one such column and is allowlisted by name. Widening that list is the escape hatch and is meant to require an argument.

context: Reading through the merge map has to decide what a merged entity's evidence is: the survivor's links, or every link in the cluster. Merging never moves an evidence_link, so the two answers differ
alternatives: (a) keep evidence_for row-scoped and add evidence_for_cluster alongside it (b) make evidence_for resolve through the merge map (c) return cluster evidence flattened, without saying which entity each link hangs on
evidence: (b) silently changes what an existing read means and leaves no way to ask the row-level question, which is the question an analyst auditing the merge itself needs. (c) discards the answer to 'which of these two records did that come from' - the question a merge makes hard to ask and ADR-0008 exists to keep answerable. a_cluster_shows_the_evidence_of_everything_in_it asserts both reads and that the cluster read attributes each link to its own entity.
selected: (a) two reads, each honest about its scope, with ClusterEvidence carrying the owning entity
consequences: A caller must choose, and choosing wrong shows the survivor's evidence only - the absorbed record's material disappearing at the moment the person was identified. That risk is the cost of not making (b) the default. The cluster read is one IN over at most the cluster's size, which the depth-1 invariant (D-020) keeps to one level.

context: open_case returned a connection and some paths, and dropped the case master key. Every existing test generated its own key and used it for both write and read, so nothing depended on the open path returning one, and the application had never actually reopened a case
alternatives: (a) return an OpenCase struct carrying conn, paths and cmk together (b) add a separate call that re-derives the key from the passphrase when bytes are needed (c) have BlobStore hold the key from construction
evidence: (b) means the passphrase is held or re-prompted for every document read, and leaves the broken state reachable by simply not making the second call - the defect this is fixing. (c) puts live key material in a long-lived object whose lifetime nobody tracks, and BlobStore is constructed from a path in a dozen places. (a) makes the incomplete case unrepresentable: there is no way to get a connection out of this crate without the key that completes it. Verified by returning a freshly generated key from finish_open: exactly the two blob-reading tests fail, at the blob layer, while every database assertion above them still passes.
selected: (a) OpenCase { conn, paths, cmk }, returned by create_case, open_case and open_case_with_recovery_key
consequences: The key is live secret material for as long as an OpenCase is held, which is the whole session. It zeroizes on drop and cannot be printed or compared in variable time, and Debug is written out rather than derived so the redaction is this crate's decision. What it must not do is escape the process: nothing serialises OpenCase, and nothing at the IPC boundary may. Twenty call sites were rewritten, all mechanical.

context: Turning a stored content hash back into readable bytes needs the wrapped key from the blob table, whose columns are nullable for a reason. The reassembly existed twice - once in kokin-extract, once copied into a test - and the layer above still had no way to do it
alternatives: (a) one blob_access in kokin-store returning Readable, Shredded or Unrecorded as values (b) leave it in kokin-extract and let callers reach for it there (c) return a BlobRef or an error, with shredded as one of the error variants (d) also check the ciphertext file and report a fourth state
evidence: (b) makes an HTML extractor the owner of a fact about storage, and the third copy is where the distinctions get collapsed. (c) makes deliberate destruction an error: shredding is a supported operation on a healthy case (docs/limitations/deletion.md), and an error is what a UI renders in red. (d) needs a BlobStore and the key, which turns a cheap database read into an I/O call and lets the function report on a file it only stat-ed - the read itself already fails with NotFound, which is a better answer because something opened the file. A/B: collapsing Shredded into Unrecorded fails the new reopen test and kokin-extract's pre-existing shredded test.
selected: (a), with kokin-extract mapping the three answers onto its own error taxonomy
consequences: kokin-store gains a dependency on kokin-blob for the BlobRef type, which is acyclic - kokin-blob depends only on kokin-keys. Err from blob_access now means a database failure and nothing else. Callers must handle three cases where they previously handled a Result, which is the point: the two ways evidence becomes unreadable have different answers and only one of them is a problem.

context: create_case returns the recovery key once and it is never stored in usable form, but a RecoveryKey is thirty-two bytes of Secret with no textual form - so every case created through the application would have had an unusable recovery path, discovered on the day it was needed
alternatives: (a) render it as Crockford base32 with a checksum and return it once from create_case (b) return raw hex (c) write it to a file beside the case (d) use a BIP-39 style wordlist
evidence: (c) puts the recovery key next to the thing it unlocks, which is not a backup. (b) is 64 characters of 0-9a-f with no confusable-character handling and no way to tell a typo from a wrong key. (d) needs a 2048-word list, a language decision, and a dependency, and its advantage is memorability that nobody should rely on for a key they must not lose. (a) is 56 characters in eight groups of seven, omits I L O U, applies Crockford read-alike substitutions on input, and carries a 24-bit BLAKE3 checksum. 24 bits rather than 20 so the encoding divides evenly into characters: with padding bits, two written forms could mean one key, which one_wrong_character_is_caught found before it shipped.
selected: (a) kokin_keys::phrase, and NewCaseView.recovery_key as the single value in the command layer that carries key material across IPC
consequences: One value in the whole IPC surface is key material, deliberately, at one moment. There is no command that returns it again - doing so would mean holding it for the session or re-deriving it, and neither is permitted here - so an interface that fails to show it has destroyed the recovery path, which the UI must make impossible to skip past. The checksum is detection, not correction, and not a second factor: the AEAD tag on the wrapped key is what makes a wrong key fail closed.

context: The session has to decide what happens when a case is opened while one is already open
alternatives: (a) refuse with CaseAlreadyOpen and require an explicit close (b) close the first and open the second (c) hold several open cases and give commands a case handle
evidence: (b) is the convenient one and the reason for A-030: every panel already rendered keeps describing a case the commands no longer act on, and filing an observation into the wrong investigation produces no error anywhere. (c) is where a multi-case product ends up, and it makes every command take a handle the interface can get wrong, which is the same failure with more surface. (a) makes changing case a thing the interface performs and can therefore reflect in what it shows.
selected: (a) one Option<OpenCase> behind a mutex, refusing rather than swapping
consequences: Comparing two cases side by side is not possible, and will need (c) or a second window when it is wanted - deliberately deferred until there is a use for it rather than designed for speculatively. A poisoned mutex, meaning a command panicked holding an open case, is reported as Internal and requires a close and reopen rather than being silently recovered from.

context: Commands returned Result<String, String>, so the only thing an interface could branch on was the text of an error message
alternatives: (a) a CommandError of a closed ErrorCode enum plus a human message (b) keep strings and have the UI match on prose (c) serialise the underlying error enums directly
evidence: (b) means a reworded message silently removes a branch - a wrong-passphrase dialog that stops appearing because someone improved the wording, which review does not catch because both changes look right. (c) couples the interface to the shape of StoreError and would carry any field a future variant gains straight to the webview, which is exactly what A-029 is about. (a) splits the machine-readable part from the human-readable one; From<StoreError> maps variant by variant rather than stringifying, so a new variant is a decision made in the layer that knows what a user can do about it.
selected: (a) CommandError { code, message } with ErrorCode as a closed snake_case enum
consequences: Adding a code is a deliberate act with a compile error attached, and Internal is documented as a bug rather than a bucket. Every command in this layer and every one added later returns this type; an error that reaches the interface without a code is not representable.

context: Coverage is the caveat that makes a result list honest, and it is a separate function from search - so an interface can render results without it, and the gap stays exactly as invisible as it was before coverage was measured
alternatives: (a) return hits and coverage in one payload with coverage non-optional (b) a separate coverage command the UI calls alongside search (c) attach coverage only when a search returns nothing (d) return coverage as an optional field
evidence: (c) is backwards: forty hits from a case that is 60% read is more misleading than none, because nobody interrogates a full page of results. (b) and (d) both make the caveat something a caller can forget, and a caveat that can be forgotten is a caveat that will be - the UI under deadline is exactly where it gets dropped. Coverage is cheap enough to compute per search: it scans lineage, which is small next to the documents it describes, and touches no full-text index.
selected: (a) SearchView { hits, total, coverage } with coverage as a plain value
consequences: Every result list carries a case-scoped statement of what the search could not reach. It is deliberately weaker than what an analyst wants - deciding whether an unread document matches a query means reading it - so the interface must present it as 'this case holds documents no search can reach' and not as a confidence in the results. A standalone coverage command exists as well, for a case overview before anyone has searched; the dependency runs the right way round.

context: kokin_search::Hit carries a relevance score, and the view layer has to decide whether the interface sees it
alternatives: (a) drop it and let the order carry the ordering (b) pass the raw BM25 value through (c) normalise it to 0-100 for display
evidence: (b) hands the webview a negative number where lower is better, on a scale that depends on the corpus - meaningless to display and dangerous to compare across queries. (c) is worse, because a percentage next to a search result reads as a confidence in the result, and this product has seven named dimensions of confidence that mean something and would now be competing with a text-similarity figure that does not. (a) keeps the only honest signal, which is the order, and it is already applied server-side before the payload is built.
selected: (a) HitView has no relevance field
consequences: An interface cannot re-sort by relevance client-side, which is correct - relevance ordering is what it already received. Sorting by anything else (date, kind) is a query concern and belongs in the search options. a_hit_carries_no_relevance_score asserts the exact field set, so adding it back is a decision with a failing test attached.

context: An entity is commonly assessed on some dimensions and not others, and the view has to decide what happens to the ones nobody has touched
alternatives: (a) always return all seven, with unassessed ones marked as such (b) return only the dimensions that have an assessment (c) return all seven and fill the gaps with the insufficient_information value as though it had been recorded
evidence: (b) is the obvious implementation and the dangerous one: a dimension that is absent from a panel reads as a dimension with nothing to worry about, which is the opposite of what an unassessed dimension means. (c) fabricates a record - it would show an assessment with no actor and no timestamp, and ADR-0007 makes insufficient_information a value somebody chooses, not a default the code supplies. (a) reports the dimension with an explicit unassessed state and an empty value list, so the interface has to render the difference between 'nobody looked' and 'somebody looked and could not tell'.
selected: (a) all seven always, agreement = unassessed | assessed | disagreed
consequences: The dimension list comes from the case's own scale table rather than from kokin_graph::scales(), so a case holding a dimension this build has never heard of still shows it and an assessment made under version 1 renders under its own labels. Where a merged cluster's rows were assessed differently, the disagreement is reported with both values attributed to their rows rather than reconciled - picking a winner is a composite score with a smaller denominator.

context: Every write records who made it, and the command layer is where that name is chosen. kokin_graph refuses rule: and ai: actors the decisions only a person may make (ADR-0008) and migration 7 refuses them again in a CHECK constraint, but the module note in kokin_graph::resolution says exactly where that ends: neither can catch automation writing actor = user:local. Here that stops being hypothetical, because a request field is written by the webview - the least trusted thing in this process, and the one that renders hostile HTML (A-031).
alternatives: (a) a single ACTOR constant, no actor field on any request type, deny_unknown_fields everywhere (b) accept actor from the caller (c) accept it but validate the prefix server-side
evidence: (b) reduces ADR-0008's refusals and migration 7's CHECK to a naming convention the caller chooses to honour: the schema would faithfully record a person where a machine acted, and the audit chain would be intact and false, which is worse than absent. (c) looks like the careful version and is not - a prefix check confirms the string is well formed, never that it is true, so it buys the appearance of validation and nothing else. (a) makes the guarantee structural: a command arriving here IS a person, because something happened in a window a human is looking at. deny_unknown_fields is the second half - without it a caller sends actor anyway, serde ignores it, and the request that tried to lie is indistinguishable from an honest one.
selected: (a) write::ACTOR as a constant, every write request deny_unknown_fields, a_request_cannot_name_its_own_actor holding it in place
consequences: MachineMayNotAct is unreachable from this crate by construction, which is a stronger statement than mapping it correctly - it is mapped anyway, because the mapping must be right for the in-process rules engine and model that will call kokin_graph under their own names, and because routing a refusal through Storage is how a deliberate boundary comes to look like a database fault. The honest cost: the actor is user:local rather than a person, because a case does not yet know who is at the keyboard, so two analysts sharing a machine are indistinguishable in the audit chain. That is coarse. Accepting the name from the webview would make every actor unverifiable instead of merely coarse, which is not a trade worth making.

context: kokin_graph accepts an empty rationale on a merge, a split and a rejection, and defaults an assessment's contributing_factors_json to []. So the command layer had to decide whether a judgement with no stated reason is a thing this product records.
alternatives: (a) refuse both at the command layer (b) accept them, as the crate below does (c) refuse in kokin_graph so the rule holds for every caller
evidence: (c) is the tempting one and it is wrong: the rules engine and the model will also call kokin_graph, and a machine-authored candidate legitimately has factors rather than prose - forcing a human rationale there would mean fabricating one. (b) leaves ADR-0007's why panel rendering a blank, and a merge whose rationale is empty cannot be reconsidered six weeks later, which is the only reason ADR-0008 went to the trouble of making merges reversible. (a) puts the rule where the actor is known to be a person (D-032): a human clicking merge can say why, and if they cannot, that is worth discovering before the merge and not after.
selected: (a) explanation() and rationale() reject empty and whitespace-only input with ExplanationRequired, at the command layer only
consequences: ExplanationRequired is a distinct code so an interface can put the cursor in the reason box rather than showing a failure. The factors list is serialised here rather than accepted as a string, so the column always holds well-formed JSON of a known shape - a caller handing over raw text would be writing prose into a field the why panel reads as structure. Trimmed before storage, so a rationale of three spaces is refused rather than stored. This is a layer rule and not a schema rule, and it is written down as one: an in-process caller can still record a judgement with no prose, which is correct for a rule and would be a lie for a person.

context: An export has to be protected by something, and the case is already protected by a passphrase-derived KEK wrapping a case master key (ADR-0015), with the database keyed by the raw CMK and the blob filenames keyed with it too.
alternatives: (a) re-wrap the same CMK under a fresh export passphrase, new salt, and drop the recovery wrap (b) reuse the case's own header unchanged (c) generate a new CMK and re-encrypt the database and every blob under it (d) re-wrap under a new passphrase and keep the source case's recovery wrap
evidence: (b) means handing someone an export hands them the case passphrase, which is the opposite of what sharing a copy should cost. (c) is the only option that gives real key separation and it costs a full rewrite of every byte of evidence, plus new blob storage names, for a property nobody has asked for - the recipient of a package is being trusted with the contents by definition. (d) is (a) with a second door: the recovery key is the one value users are told to write on paper, so keeping its wrap would make every package ever produced retroactively openable the day that paper is photographed. (a) also happens to be nearly free, because rotate_passphrase already proves changing the wrap does not require touching case data.
selected: (a) kokin_export::package writes a header with a fresh salt, the CMK wrapped under an export passphrase, and cmk_wrapped_by_recovery = None
consequences: A package has no recovery path at all - lose the export passphrase and that package is gone. Correct for a copy, indefensible for a case, which is why the two headers differ here and nowhere else. Key separation is explicitly not achieved: the CMK is the same key, so anyone holding the source case's header and passphrase can decrypt a package made from it. Stated in the module documentation rather than left to be inferred from the code. The aad still binds the case id, so a package is the same case and cannot be silently relabelled as a different one.

context: A package is one file holding a manifest, a header, a database and N blobs, and something has to frame those entries.
alternatives: (a) a purpose-built sequential container with a closed set of legal entry names (b) tar (c) zip (d) a directory rather than a single file
evidence: (d) is what a case already is, and ADR-0016 committed to export producing a single verifiable file for transport. (b) and (c) bring arbitrary paths, symlinks, hardlinks and compression - which is to say zip-slip, writes outside the destination, and decompression bombs, a class this project already wrote a limiter for in increment 4. Every one of those features would be imported solely in order to be restricted again, and each restriction is a place to get it wrong. The payload is AEAD ciphertext and a SQLCipher database, so compression buys nothing anyway. (a) replaces all of it with a whitelist: entry names are a closed enum parsed by exact match or a strict 64-hex address, so a path is not a value the format can express.
selected: (a) crates/kokin-export/src/container.rs - magic KOKINPKG1, LE length prefixes, EntryName as the only constructor from wire bytes
consequences: Extraction cannot be tricked into writing outside the destination because it never composes a path from untrusted bytes: the destination is chosen by matching on the enum. a_name_that_is_not_on_the_list_is_refused pins the refusals, including uppercase hex, which would be one file on Windows and two on Linux. The cost is a format no other tool reads, so a package cannot be opened with unzip in an emergency - accepted, because the contents are encrypted and unreadable without the passphrase regardless. Reading a package twice-over during assembly is a known inefficiency recorded in the increment report.
reversibility: hard once packages exist in the field
